title: Back-of-Envelope Fundamentals
summary: The reference latency numbers, powers-of-two shortcuts, and rounding habits behind every estimate you'll make later — QPS, storage, bandwidth — in a system-design interview.

slides.markdown:
Back-of-envelope estimation is quick, rough arithmetic — QPS, storage, bandwidth — done on a whiteboard to size a system before you design it. It's not about precision; it's about knowing which numbers matter and which don't.

Think of a chef eyeballing portions before cooking for 200 guests: no kitchen scale for every ingredient, but a solid sense of roughly how much rice feeds one person. This topic gives you the reference numbers and mental-math shortcuts every later estimate in this track leans on.

slides.sectionTitle: Why estimation matters before you design anything
slides.markdown:
An interviewer asks you to estimate scale before you design because the right architecture depends entirely on the numbers. A service handling 1,000 requests a day runs fine on a single small Postgres instance. The same service at 1 billion requests a day — roughly 11,600 requests per second on average (1,000,000,000 ÷ 86,400 seconds) — needs caching, read replicas, and probably sharding before a line of code is written.

Skip the estimate and you risk designing an elaborate distributed system for a workload that never needed one, or the reverse: a simple design that falls over the moment it ships.

Estimate first, then let the design match the number — never the other way around.

A handful of rounded latency numbers cover most estimation questions you'll face. You don't need seven decimal places — you need the right order of magnitude.

| Operation | Approx. latency |
|---|---|
| Read from RAM | ~100 ns |
| Random read from SSD | ~100 µs (~1,000x RAM) |
| Round trip within one datacenter | ~0.5 ms |
| Disk seek (spinning HDD) | ~10 ms |
| Round trip across regions (e.g. US ↔ Europe) | ~150 ms |

Each row is roughly an order of magnitude slower than the one above it. That's the shape to memorize — RAM is fast, disk and cross-region network are the two things that will dominate any latency budget you're asked to reason about.

slides.sectionTitle: Powers of two and ten: fast mental math shortcuts
slides.markdown:
Storage and memory come in powers of two; humans think in powers of ten. The bridge: **2^10 ≈ 10^3** (1,024 vs 1,000, about 2.4% off), and that approximation compounds cleanly — **2^20 ≈ 10^6** (mega), **2^30 ≈ 10^9** (giga), **2^40 ≈ 10^12** (tera).

Use it to convert fast: 2 billion (2×10^9) records at 500 bytes each is 10^12 bytes. Divide by 10^9 bytes/GB (the 2^30 shortcut) and you get 1,000 GB — 1 TB — without touching a calculator.

The error from this approximation is under 10% even at 2^40, which is nothing next to the uncertainty already baked into your traffic and growth assumptions.

slides.sectionTitle: Diagram: the latency numbers ladder (L1 cache to cross-region)
slides.markdown:
<<< Image: vertical ladder diagram with rungs from bottom to top — L1 cache reference (~1 ns), main memory (~100 ns), random SSD read (~100 µs), same-datacenter round trip (~0.5 ms), disk seek (~10 ms), cross-region round trip (~150 ms) — each rung labelled with its latency and the approximate multiplier over the rung below it >>>

Lay the numbers from the previous slide out as a ladder and the jumps matter more than the absolute values: memory to SSD is roughly a 1,000x jump, and a cross-region round trip is roughly 300x slower than one that stays inside your own datacenter (150 ms vs 0.5 ms).

Every time a design crosses one of these rungs — hitting SSD instead of a cache, routing cross-region instead of serving from a regional replica — that's where the latency budget gets spent.

slides.sectionTitle: Rounding strategy: precision you don't need vs precision you do
slides.markdown:
Two different kinds of rounding show up in every estimate, and mixing them up is the most common beginner mistake. **Rounding for speed** is safe: treating a day as 100,000 seconds instead of 86,400 is about 16% high (100,000 ÷ 86,400 ≈ 1.157), which never flips a decision between needing 10 servers or 100. **Rounding away a real multiplier** is not safe: dropping a replication factor of 3 or an index overhead of 40% changes your storage total by that same factor, and the design decision can change with it.

Before you round something to zero, ask whether it's noise (safe) or a real cost that scales with the system (not safe).

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: chasing decimal precision that doesn't change the design
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "My storage estimate came out between 47 TB and 48 TB — I need to nail down the exact figure before I can keep designing."

**Why it's wrong:** both 47 TB and 48 TB are far past what a single machine holds, so the actual decision — multi-node storage, probably sharded — is identical either way. Time spent narrowing the third significant figure buys zero additional design clarity.

**Correct model:** estimate to one significant figure and move on. Only go back for more precision when a number sits near an actual decision boundary — for example, right at the edge of what fits on one large instance versus needing to shard at all.
